_meta.scope: Rules for the cellar (wine) and quors (spirits) tasting-menu builder: pour order, prep timeline, small bites.
_meta.method: Every URL in 'sources' was opened during research. Text is paraphrased. Numbers are as the source states them; F/C conversions are marked. Ranges reflect disagreement between sources; items marked contested, inferred or low_confidence are flagged.

principles.rule: Open with sparkling (or a crisp white).
principles.why: Dr. Vinny's suggested dinner sequence starts with bubbles or a crisp white; Wine Folly suggests a sparkling wine or simple wine cocktail as guests arrive. Sparkling also shows best soon after opening, while its mousse is fresh.

principles.rule: Go from light-bodied and delicate to full-bodied and rich.
principles.why: Every source treats body as the main axis: a big wine tasted first makes the next lighter wine seem thin. Jancis Robinson calls light-to-full the sensible general approach; SAQ suggests ordering guests' bottles from least to most intense.

principles.rule: Whites before reds (convention, not law).
principles.why: Lighter-to-heavier usually means whites first, which Dr. Vinny calls the near-universal approach; Jancis Robinson notes nothing is sacrosanct about it.

principles.rule: Aromatic/fragrant whites before oaked whites.
principles.why: Andy Howard MW groups fragrant whites ahead of oaky ones, part of delicate-before-rich.

principles.rule: Low tannin before high tannin.
principles.why: Tannin lingers on the palate and carries over into the next wine, making delicate wines hard to read afterwards; start with a wine that is not very tannic.

principles.rule: Dry before sweet, both across the flight and within each colour group.
principles.why: Sugar coats the palate and lingers, so a dry wine after a sweet one tastes sharp, bitter or sour.

principles.rule: Young before old (default for verticals).
principles.why: Dr. Vinny calls youngest-to-oldest the more common approach, following how a wine develops toward complexity.
principles.exception: Oldest-to-youngest is also valid: older wines are often softer and lighter, so starting with them lets body and tannin build gradually.

principles.rule: Sweet and fortified wines last.
principles.why: Because sweetness carries over, dessert and fortified wines close the flight. Jancis Robinson serves sweet wine as a small glass at the end and prefers cheese before anything sweet. If there are white and red dessert wines, the whites can come first.

principles.rule: Cheese course before dessert.
principles.why: Jancis Robinson often finishes the dry main-course wine with cheese and then moves to anything sweet.

exceptions.rule: Sparkling can appear mid-flight or at the end as a palate refresher.
exceptions.why: Andy Howard MW describes sparkling as palate-refreshing and does not require it to go first; the reader in that Q&A notes events typically pour it first and dessert wines last, which the answer does not insist on.

exceptions.rule: Reds before whites is defensible for tired palates.
exceptions.why: Andy Howard MW often prefers red before white because a fresh white is easier to judge late in a long tasting. This directly contradicts the whites-first convention.

exceptions.rule: A light red may precede a full, rich white.
exceptions.why: The Court of Master Sommeliers food-and-wine material says a red can be followed by a white if the white is richer; Dr. Vinny notes long casual meals can switch between colours without harm. But SAQ and Dr. Vinny's dinner sequence both put fuller whites before light reds, so treat this as an option ordered by body, not a default.

exceptions.rule: Some sweet whites (and young Sauternes) can open a meal.
exceptions.why: SAQ notes some fruity, sweet whites suit the start of a meal. Sommelier Will Predhomme (quoted by Decanter) suggests young Sauternes as an aperitif and older (10 to 15+ year) Sauternes later.

exceptions.rule: Pace and food loosen the rules.
exceptions.why: Dr. Vinny: fewer wines tasted slowly suffer less carryover, and food on the table changes how the palate resets. Keep the strict order for focused tastings or many wines.

exceptions.rule: Alternative: order purely by residual sugar.
exceptions.why: Dr. Vinny's blind tastings sometimes sort all wines by rising residual sugar regardless of colour.

placement_of_app_styles.note: Default slots built from the principles above. Where no source names a style's position (rose, orange), the placement is an inference from body/tannin and the source-given serving temperature; it is marked inferred.

inferred.rose: No source places rose explicitly. Wine Folly gives rose the same serving range as full-bodied whites (44-55 F / 7-12 C), so it sits among the whites by body.
inferred.orange: No source places orange wine. It is skin-macerated and can be tannic (Wine Folly cites tannins; Decanter separates heavier tannic examples), so the tannin rule puts it after the whites and before or among the light reds; lighter orange wines can move earlier.

tie_breaks.rule: If two wines share a slot, put the lower-sweetness one first.
Then lighter body / lower intensity first.
Then younger before older (allow the reverse for old, faded reds).
Keep pairs of related wines (e.g. same grape, two regions) side by side so they can be compared.
If several wines exceed 14.5% ABV, shrink pours or add breaks instead of reordering.

principles.rule: Aperitifs (vermouth, bitter aperitivo, dry sherry-style) belong at the start of a session; bitter digestivo/amaro belongs at the end.
principles.why: Difford's defines the aperitif as a pre-meal, appetite-stimulating drink; Punch frames neat amaro and digestivo as after-dinner pours that act as a foil to a rich meal.

principles.rule: Open with a familiar, mid-weight benchmark.
principles.why: Whisky Advocate's flight plan starts with a median-style whisky that calibrates the palate: not too strong, too light or too odd.

principles.rule: Lower ABV/proof to higher ABV/proof.
principles.why: Whisky Advocate says strength should generally build through the flight, so the strongest whisky usually closes it, with exceptions for dominant-flavour bottles. Beefeater's gin-tasting guide runs lowest-proof to highest-proof. Sip Tequila orders by intensity (lightest to richest) rather than strictly by proof, but moves any unusually high-proof expression later.

principles.rule: Lighter and delicate before full-bodied and rich.
principles.why: Difford's arranges samples by flavour intensity, lightest first, bold or smoky last.

principles.rule: Unaged/younger before aged/older.
principles.why: Sip Tequila's vertical runs Blanco, Reposado, Anejo, Extra Anejo; Difford's runs vertical tastings youngest to oldest.

principles.rule: Non-aromatic before aromatic (e.g. grappa, pisco).
principles.why: Difford's specifically recommends tasting non-aromatic grappa and pisco before aromatic ones.

principles.rule: Unpeated before peated/smoky; dominant flavours (heavy peat, heavy sherry) go late.
principles.why: Difford's places smoky spirits last and orders Scotch malts Lowland, Highland, Speyside, Island, Islay. Whisky Advocate puts dominant-flavour whiskies in the last slots, where they may outrank proof.

principles.rule: Sweet liqueurs and cream liqueurs last.
principles.why: Inferred, not directly stated by a spirits source: the wine sources' reason (sugar coats the palate and makes dry drinks taste harsh afterwards) applies equally, and Whisky Advocate's tasting-food guidance saves sweets for the end because they are 'palate killers' early.

water.rule: Taste neat first, then add water a few drops at a time and reassess.
water.why: Whisky Advocate, Difford's, Decanter (gin) and Beefeater all start neat. Use a pipette or eyedropper (Whisky Advocate) and keep the same dilution across samples (Difford's).

water.rule: High-strength and cask-strength spirits benefit most from water.
water.why: Whisky Advocate says cask strength often benefits; Master of Malt says higher-ABV whiskies usually benefit more. Difford's suggests diluting high-strength spirits with up to about a quarter water (it writes '25% water (1:4)'; note 1 part water to 4 parts spirit is 20% water, while 25% water is 1:3) and warns that production samples at 70% ABV or above could be harmful neat.

water.rule: When comparing spirits of different strengths, dilute them to roughly equal strength.
water.why: Difford's recommends this so the alcohol difference does not dominate the comparison.
SWA: a little still, unchilled water. Whisky Advocate: room temperature, avoid strongly mineral water. Master of Malt: room temperature; cold water can numb the palate.
Whisky Advocate calls it personal; it cites master blenders working at about 20% ABV and Booker Noe saying bourbon can go up to 1:1 with water, as examples rather than rules.

tie_breaks.rule: Proof differences of 1-2 percentage points are negligible; swap freely for flavour reasons.
A dominant flavour (heavy peat or sherry) can outrank proof and take the last slot.
Keep a theme (one category) where possible; contrast flights are a second option.
Use at most six; Difford's says the palate may tire after six, and Whisky Advocate recommends no more than six even for experienced tasters.

spark.note: Wine Folly lets high-quality sparkling such as vintage Champagne warm up a little (no duration given).

crisp.note: Sources disagree. Wine Folly's chart gives 38-45 F (3-7 C) for light whites, but its Sauvignon Blanc page says 45-55 F (7-12 C) and its unoaked-Chardonnay page about 45 F (7 C). Wine Spectator gives 40-50 F for whites, with lighter whites at the cooler end. Wine Folly's party guide uses 45-55 F (7-13 C) for all whites.

arom.note: Wine Folly's Riesling page uses the light-white range.

full.note: Oaked Chardonnay is about 55 F (12 C) per Wine Folly. Wine Spectator puts fuller whites at the warmer end of 40-50 F.

orange.note: Decanter: lighter, short-maceration orange wines at 10-12 C (about 50-54 F); heavier, tannic ones tasted at 12-14 C (about 54-57 F) and warmed toward room temperature if they seem closed; mature examples a little warmer. Wine Folly: 55-60 F (12-15 C). F values for Decanter's figures are converted.

mred.note: Wine Folly's chart groups light and medium reds at 55-60 F (12-15 C), but its Merlot page says 60-68 F (15-20 C).

fred.note: Wine Spectator gives 60-65 F in one answer and 60-70 F in another; Wine Folly 60-68 F.

sweet.note: Wine Folly only says it depends on style. Decanter: Aline Baly serves Sauternes/Barsac at 9-10 C (cooler for spicy or sweet dishes and for very young or very old vintages); Heidi Schroeck serves Austrian Auslese/BA/TBA/Ausbruch at 12-14 C. F values are converted. With spicy food, Wine Folly's test favoured an ice-cold, low-alcohol sweet white.

fino_manzanilla.guidance: Well chilled / straight from the fridge.

cream_sherry_sweet_oloroso.guidance: Sweet oloroso and cream sherry: chilled, in a tulip-shaped glass. PX needs no chilling; pour it over crushed ice or vanilla ice cream.

sherry_general_wine_folly.note: Wine Folly gives one range for all sherry, which conflicts with the fino/manzanilla advice above.

rule_of_thumb.guidance: Richer, older fortified wines warmer; lighter, fresher ones cooler.

fridge_timing.rule: A food fridge runs about 35-40 F (about 2-4 C), colder than any serving range above.
Bottle chilled in a food fridge: take it out 30-60 minutes before serving.
Ice-and-water bucket (or a large bowl): chills a bottle in 20-30 minutes.
Reds: Dr. Vinny sometimes gives a red about 10 minutes in an ice bucket before serving; serve reds slightly cool (60-70 F) since wine above about 72 F can taste hot and dull.
Wine warms in the glass, so err slightly cool.
Reds stored in the fridge can taste flat until they warm; Wine Folly gives no minutes.
Opened Port: refrigerate to extend life, then let it come nearly to room temperature before pouring.

spark.note: Wine Folly gives no decant time; for fine young vintage Champagne it suggests a coupe or Burgundy-style glass if bubbles mask flavour.

arom.note: Decanting can harm highly aromatic whites.

full.note: Only for full-bodied, cool-climate whites (e.g. white Burgundy) showing a funky, steamed-mushroom note; Wine Folly's Chardonnay page says decanting is generally only for very old Chardonnay.

orange.note: Decanter's orange-wine answer does not discuss decanting.

lred.note: Pinot Noir and Gamay: about 30 minutes.

mred.note: Wine Folly's decanting guide: Zinfandel, Malbec, Grenache blends and Sangiovese about 30 minutes; medium reds such as Cabernet Franc, Dolcetto and Montepulciano about 1 hour; Merlot (grouped with Cabernet/Bordeaux) 60+ minutes. Wine Folly's Merlot page instead says about 30 minutes, so Merlot timing is contested. Taste periodically.

fred.note: Cabernet/Bordeaux, Syrah, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Mourvedre, Petite Sirah: 60+ minutes; very tannic Aglianico, Barbera, Sagrantino: 3+ hours.

sweet.note: No source recommended decanting sweet table wines.

fort.note: Symington (via Decanter): only vintage Port needs decanting. Wine Folly lists 30 minutes for vintage Port and Madeira, but Blandy's (via Decanter) says no Madeira needs decanting, and Wine Folly's general Port and Sherry pages say no.

caveats.rule: The younger and more tannic the wine, the longer it needs.
Dry wines aged 20+ years: decant just before serving (to separate sediment, not to aerate).
Watch for sediment with a candle or phone light; a stainless filter helps.
Decanting cannot be undone; most decanted reds last about 12-18 hours; a vinegar smell means it went too long.
Aerators are faster but not advised for aged wines.
Taste young wines periodically rather than trusting a fixed time.
Decant bold reds before the event, out of sight of guests if you prefer.

temperature.rule: Taste spirits at room temperature; chilling suppresses aroma. Cupping the glass warms it slightly.
Hold the glass by the stem or base if you don't want to warm the spirit.
Room for a cognac tasting: about 20 C (68 F). That figure is for the room, not the spirit.
Exception, herbal liqueur: Chartreuse as a digestif is served chilled at 11-13 C (about 52-55 F, converted) or over ice; chill the bottle a few hours ahead; do not freeze it.
Exception, unaged brandy: blanche Armagnac is served ice-cold.
Vermouth: refrigerate after opening. Difford's says keep no more than six weeks; Wine Spectator says up to a few months refrigerated, with oxidation noticeable after about two weeks in a cabinet.
Cream liqueur (Baileys): the producer says an opened bottle needs no refrigeration if kept at 32-77 F out of direct sun. No opened source gave a serving temperature.
Vodka: Difford's assesses vodka at room temperature. No opened source supported a chilled-vodka tasting standard, though the zakuski tradition is shot-then-bite.

glassware.rule: Tulip-shaped nosing glass (Glencairn or copita) for whisky and most neat spirits: the bowl allows swirling and the narrowed rim concentrates aroma.
ISO tasting glass (21.5 cl / 7.25 oz) or a small wine glass is an acceptable substitute.
Gin: copa or rounded tasting glass; avoid highball, rocks and shot glasses for tasting.
Mezcal: traditional copita, jicara or veladora rather than a shot glass.
Vermouth on its own: a wine glass.
Same size and shape of glass for everyone and every pour; one glass per spirit, plus a spare if comparing with and without water.
Sniff each empty glass for detergent or cloth smells first.

detail.value: about 1 oz (about 30 ml), or enough to taste a few times
2-3 cl tasting measures (Armagnac, after a meal: two measures of different Armagnacs)
2-4 cl into a tulip glass (cognac; seen only as a related-article teaser on the page, so lower confidence)

pour_size.note: ml/oz range combines the sources; 0.5 oz is about 15 ml and 50 ml is about 1.7 oz (converted). For 6+ spirits or anything high-proof, use the low end.

standard_drink_reference.value: US standard drink = 14 g alcohol = 1.5 fl oz of 40% ABV spirit

rest_time.rule: Return to a sample after 15-20 minutes to see how it has developed; cover waiting samples with a watch glass or plain paper.
Aromas change as the spirit takes in air; wait a few minutes between sips to judge the finish; rest your nose if it tires.
Allow at least 10 minutes per whisky in a flight.
No opened source gave a wait time after adding water; Master of Malt just says swirl, then taste.

palate_cleansers.item: Water biscuits / water or oyster crackers
Plain white bread or bread cubes
Sniffing coffee beans or a sip of cold weak coffee (gin tasting)
Smelling the inside of your arm to reset the nose

bitters.rule: Bitters are not poured for sipping; to taste them, add a few dashes (1 dash is about 1/8 tsp) to soda water and stir.

na.rule: Tasting NA spirits neat is a weak guide to how they perform mixed; consider tasting them in a simple standard drink (Alcademics used a Daiquiri format) alongside a neat taste.

liqueur.rule: Neat amaro is a classic digestivo pour; shaking amaro over ice or adding hot water (amaro caldo) are alternatives.

pour_size.value: 2-3 oz (about 60-90 ml), about half a normal glass
fill no glass more than a third full

pours_per_750ml.value: about 8 normal pours; about 15 for a social tasting of 6-8 wines

standard_drink.value: 5 fl oz of 12% wine = 1 US standard drink (so a 750 ml bottle is about 5 standard pours, by arithmetic)

buy_per_guest.value: 8-10 guests: two bottles of each wine, plus a little extra, because pours get heavier after the second wine
Dinner: about half a bottle per head typically; about a bottle per head for a serious wine dinner as a buffer; thirsty guests may drink 1-2 bottles over a four-hour meal (Dan Keeling, quoted)

glasses.value: Enough identical glasses for each guest to taste two wines side by side
At least one glass per person; a separate water glass each; if a white follows a red in the same glass, rinse it with water (or use fresh glasses) so the white doesn't look pinkish
Rental glassware runs about $1-3 per glass

pours_per_750ml.value: about 15 at 50 ml, 25 at 30 ml (1 oz), 30 at 25 ml, 50 at 15 ml (0.5 oz)
pours_per_750ml.note: Arithmetic from the pour sizes in spirits_serving.pour_size, not a figure any source states.

glasses.value: One glass per spirit per guest, plus one extra for water comparisons

buy_per_guest.value: No opened source gave a per-guest bottle count for spirits; derive from pours (number of spirits x pour size x guests) plus a margin.

flight_size.value: Whisky: no more than six per sitting, even for experienced tasters; as few as two works
Spirits: the palate may tire after six; ten is a lot

flight_size.note: The app allows 3-8 bottles; above six, warn and suggest smaller pours or a break.

pacing.value: Whisky: at least 10 minutes per whisky
Structured whisky tasting: about an hour of quiet tasting, then about 30 minutes of discussion before reveal
High-alcohol wines (several above 14.5% ABV): smaller pours or longer breaks

spit_dump.value: A personal spittoon per guest (e.g. an opaque cup), plus a shared dump bucket; spitting is normal
An empty cup per taster, or an ice bucket or large container
Use a spit bucket when tasting several whiskies

food_timing.value: Critical tasting: only plain crackers or bread during the pours, cheese or plain chips on the side; bring out most food after everyone has finished their notes
Social tasting: food throughout; sweets and desserts last
Keep food simple, self-serve and one-hand: cheese, fresh fruit, bread, cured meats; avoid spicy, vinegary or sweet foods that distort wine
During an agave tasting, hold spicy, strongly citrusy and salty snacks until the end
Neutral, absorbent food (bread, breadsticks, cheese biscuits) cushions the alcohol
Place snacks near the spirits they suit (pecans near bourbon, Stilton near peated Scotch)

environment.value: Well-lit room, few distractions; ask guests to skip heavy perfume or cologne
Open each bottle when it is its turn

responsible_serving.value: Water on the table and between pours
Serve plenty of food; use measured pours, one drink at a time
Decide in advance when to stop serving (e.g. an hour before the end), then switch to coffee and dessert
Have guests arrange sober drivers or rides; keep cab numbers handy; be ready to host overnight; don't let anyone drive impaired
Serve alcohol only to guests 21 and over (US)
Dilute anything at 70% ABV or above before tasting

Show standard-drink totals: 5 fl oz of 12% wine or 1.5 fl oz of 40% spirit = 1 US standard drink (14 g / 0.6 fl oz pure alcohol). By arithmetic: a 2-3 oz tasting pour of 12% wine is about 0.4-0.6 standard drinks; a 1 oz pour of 40% spirit is about 0.67 (about 0.83 at 50% ABV); a six-spirit flight of 1 oz pours at 40% is about 4 standard drinks per guest.
UK: 25 ml of 40% spirit = 1 unit; 50 ml = 2 units

open_bottle_life.value: Fino sherry and vintage Port: a couple of days; tawny Port and amontillado: months; Madeira: hardly goes off
Ruby/reserve Port 3-4 weeks; tawny up to 6 weeks refrigerated; vintage Port fades within 3 days; sweet oloroso up to 3 months refrigerated; PX from one year to the next
Most Ports stay fresh about a week after opening
open_bottle_life.note: Shorter than the Symington figures above.

open_bottle_life.value: Sauternes: more than a week; Auslese about 10 days; Ausbruch up to three weeks

principles.rule: Match weight: neither the food nor the drink should overpower the other. A light wine needs high acid or strong flavour to stand up to a rich dish.
Acid in the drink should meet or exceed acid in the food, or the wine tastes flat or flabby. Acidic wines cut fat and balance sweetness.
Fat and protein soften tannin, so fatty bites suit tannic reds. Crisp, acidic wines also cut fat by contrast.
Salty food likes some sweetness and softens tannin.
The drink must be at least as sweet as the food, or it tastes bitter. Sweet food needs a sweeter wine.

Spicy heat: residual sugar and low alcohol calm the burn; alcohol amplifies it. Wine Folly's informal test favoured an ice-cold, low-alcohol sweet white and found sweet, high-alcohol Port and bourbon poor with spice; bold dry reds coped better than expected.
Fish oils clash with tannin; tannic wine with oily fish can taste metallic. Red wine generally doesn't pair well with fish, except rich, mild fish.
Red wine and chocolate is a hard pairing (bitter on bitter).

Chocolate with whisky: match the oak/vanilla level (bourbon and vanilla-rich chocolate); higher cacao for smokier whiskies; fruity single-origin chocolate for sherried malts. Dark chocolate for rich drams, milk for lighter ones.

Cheese with whisky: match intensity (delicate goat and sheep cheeses with lighter whiskies), look for shared notes, and use sweeter, bolder whiskies against the salt and acid of bloomy rinds. SWA: hard cheese with robust malt, soft creamy cheese with smooth blends, blue with Islay.
Cheese before dessert, and the cheese wine need not be red; sweet wines and hard mild cheeses (Gouda, Emmental, Cheddar, Parmesan) are reliable.
Contrast or commonality: Master of Malt's shorthand is salty with sweet, smoke with fat, spice with citrus.
Regional pairings (wine and food from the same place) are a reliable starting template. Complementary pairings are safer than contrasting ones.
Sauces and seasoning drive the match more than the protein.
Oak overwhelms food easily; iron-rich greens can taste metallic with wine.
Aperitivo bites should be salty, hand-held, one or two bites, and light enough not to replace dinner.
Sweetness in dessert softens a brandy's bite.
Peated whisky needs assertive, slightly smoky, not-too-sweet food; delicate foods get overpowered.

spark.note: Crunch and salt suit racy blanc de blancs.
High-acid Champagne cuts fat; with spicy (e.g. Korean-style) chicken choose a higher-dosage or demi-sec.
Wine Folly matches spreadable goat cheese with Cremant de Loire.

crisp.note: Sauvignon Blanc's acidity and herbal notes are Wine Folly's top goat-cheese match.
Listed for both Sauvignon Blanc and unoaked Chardonnay/Chablis.

crisp.bite: Feta or burrata with fresh herbs
crisp.note: Soft, flavourful cheeses and green herbs suit Sauvignon Blanc.

arom.bite: Spicy Asian bites (e.g. Thai or Indian snacks)
arom.note: Off-dry Riesling with spicy Indian and Asian food; sweetness meets salt and heat.
Wine Folly lists both with Riesling.
Wine Folly lists pork and bacon with Riesling.

full.note: Rich, starchy vegetables for oaked styles.

rose.note: Michel Roux Jr's match for a pale Pinot Noir-based Sancerre rose.
Lighter roses suit delicate food such as charcuterie and fresh salads.

orange.bite: Roast meat bites with sage or rosemary
orange.note: Wine Folly: savoury flavours and tannin suit roasted meats and resinous herbs.
Fiona Beckett (qvevri-aged amber wine). The page was largely paywalled, so this comes from a linked item on it.
Appear only as tags on Beckett's paywalled orange-wine page.

lred.note: The classic Pinot Noir match: acidity cuts the fat.
Earthy mushroom dishes flatter Pinot Noir, especially Old World styles.
Pinot is light enough for salmon.
Wine Folly: Oregon Pinot with local cow's-milk cheese (regional match); Pinot with firm goat cheddar.

mred.bite: Herbed potato croquettes and roasted tomatoes
mred.note: Wine Folly's Sangiovese example: fat tames tannin, and cherry and tomato flavours align.
Wine Folly picks Merlot for deeper, earthier goat cheese.

mred.bite: Mini lasagna or cheesy pasta bites

fred.note: Tannin plus fat; Wine Folly calls this the classic starting point.
Peppery sauces suit Cabernet; Wine Folly pairs high-alcohol Zinfandel with pepper steak.

fred.bite: Hard, mild cheese (aged Cheddar, Gouda, Parmesan shards)
fred.note: General wine-friendly cheeses; fat and protein soften tannin.

sweet.note: Decanter: thin cured ham with Sauternes is optimal (sweet against salt); Schroeck pairs prosciutto with Spatlese.
Heidi Schroeck pairs it with Beerenauslese.
Aline Baly (Sauternes) and Schroeck (apple tart with rosemary); the wine must be sweeter than the dessert.

sweet.bite: Oysters with chilli black bean sauce
sweet.note: Decanter's surprise Sauternes match; the wine's acidity balances its sweetness.

fort.note: With vintage and tawny Port and sweeter Madeiras; Wine Folly calls Port with blue cheese exceptional. Symington prefers creamy cheese over Stilton for mature vintage Port.
Fino sherry and drier Madeiras with tapas.
Wine Folly's tawny Port example (salt with sweet).
Ruby/reserve Port with cheese or dark chocolate (Symington).

fino_manzanilla.bite: Smoked, fried or grilled fish or vegetables

px_cream.bite: PX poured over vanilla ice cream

ruby_vintage_port.bite: Dark chocolate / chocolate pudding (young vintage or LBV)

whiskey.note: Master of Malt treats cheese as the default. Speyside malts suit mature firm cheddar (Whisky Advocate).
Brings out sweetness and caramel notes.

whiskey.bite: Dark chocolate for rich whiskies, milk chocolate for lighter ones

whiskey.note: Earthy profiles; roasted almonds with sherried malt.

bourbon.note: Rich, fatty, sweet foods for full-bodied bourbon.

rye.note: Bold, well-seasoned foods; avoid wing-level heat.
From Whisky Advocate's club guide. Its cheese primer warns against straight rye with goat or sheep cheese, so this is contested.

peated_smoky.note: Islay with blue (SWA); peaty Island malt with Stilton (Whisky Advocate).
Master of Malt's taste-test winner was salted peanuts ('smoky peanut butter').
High-cacao, low-fruit chocolate for bold smoky whiskies (Whisky Advocate pairs Ardbeg 10 with 90%).
Assertive, slightly smoky, not too sweet.

sherried.note: Sherry notes play off nutty cheese.
Master of Malt's snack winner for sherried malt.

irish_canadian_blended.note: Whisky Advocate's club guide says 50-65%; its chocolate primer pairs light Irish with 60-70%.

irish_canadian_blended.bite: Washed-rind cheese with a subtle, toffee-ish blend

light_floral_japanese.note: For light, crisp or citrusy whiskies.

high_proof.note: No opened source gave high-proof-specific bites. Apply the water guidance first (spirits_order.water). Wine Folly's general principle that high alcohol can offset fatty dishes, and the spice principle that alcohol amplifies heat, both apply: avoid spicy bites and lean toward fatty ones.

unaged.note: For unaged brandy, the Armagnac interprofession pairs ice-cold blanche Armagnac with smoked salmon, caviar, foie gras, cold meats and lemon tart. For white rum, Fiona Beckett's suggestions (made via cocktails) are shrimp, fish tacos and ceviche. No opened source gave sipping-specific bites for blanco tequila or new-make whisky.

agave.bite: Orange slices with sal de gusano
agave.note: Traditional mezcal accompaniment: bite the orange, then sip.
Master of Malt's favourite pairing overall, with reposado tequila.

agave.bite: Fresh cheese, melon or mango slices
Plain crackers or white bread (during the tasting)
agave.note: Sip Tequila says to hold spicy, citrusy and salty snacks until after the tasting. That conflicts with the orange-and-salt tradition, so serve those afterwards or as a separate stage.

rum.note: Master of Malt's dark-rum winner: lightness against heavy fruit, sweet against salty.

brandy.bite: Blue cheese (Roquefort, Fourme) with young Armagnac
Dark chocolate, chocolate mousse or chocolate cake (cognac.com suggests dark chocolate for older cognacs)

gin.note: Master of Malt found no clear winner for gin; olives, plantain chips and pretzels came closest.

vodka.note: Zakuski tradition: a bite always follows the drink.

vodka.bite: Smoked or pickled herring, salmon or sturgeon
Caviar on buttered blini with sour cream
Bread with salted butter and cold cuts

other.note: The 'other' category (aquavit, baijiu, shochu, anise spirits and similar) had no category-wide pairing source among those opened. Use the general principles and plain cleansers, and taste non-aromatic before aromatic (Difford's). Per-spirit food fields in spirits.json should take precedence.

liqueur.note: Little category-wide sourcing. Serve last. Any dessert should be no sweeter than the liqueur (sweetness rule). Herbal digestifs and amaro work as palate cleansers after a rich meal (Punch). Chartreuse's producer gives no food pairing.

bites.bite: Dessert no sweeter than the liqueur

bites.note: Armagnac with coffee (cafe gascon) shows the coffee-and-digestif custom; extending it to liqueurs is an inference.

aperitif.note: Salt suits the citrus and bubbles of a spritz.

aperitif.bite: Crostini or bruschetta (e.g. whipped baccala, white beans)

bitters.note: Bitters are a seasoning, not a pour: taste a few dashes in soda water. No food pairing source. In a tasting, place them as a palate-reset interlude or alongside aperitifs.

na.note: No pairing source among those opened. Pair by the profile the NA spirit imitates (botanical with the gin bites, agave-style with the agave bites); this is an inference. Alcademics found neat tasting a poor predictor of mixed performance and singled out Three Spirit Nightcap as suited to after-dinner service.
